content:
Good morning,

Although I have had an account for five years, this is the first time I have used it in any serious way. As I work in the field of nonlinear hyperbolic PDEs, I am very interested in having as many known results as possible formalised in mathlib4. A few months ago, Armstrong and Kempe formalised Sobolev spaces to some extent (apparently only on an open subset of ℝⁿ).

How would this code need to be modified (it was partly generated with an LLM) for it to be incorporated into mathlib4?

There has been interest in formalising Sobolev spaces (see https://github.com/leanprover-community/project-intentions/issues/15), but I'm not sure how ongoing this is (@Michael Rothgang ).

Generally though, upstreaming a big amount of LLM code to mathlib is not well liked and rarely (if ever) done for a variety of reasons.

Indeed, @Floris van Doorn, @Filippo A. E. Nuccio and I are working on defining Sobolev spaces in the proper generality suitable for mathlib. Our current code is in https://github.com/grunweg/SobolevSlobodeckij. We have worked on this much in the past three months, but intend to return to this soon. (Note also that @Moritz Doll has formalised a different definition of Sobolev spaces (i.e., Bessel potential spaces), which is in mathlib already. Proving the equivalence of these definitions should naturally be in mathlib, at some point.

"Zn" == Zulip notifications <noreply@zulip.com> writes:

Felix Pernegger:

There has been interest in formalising Sobolev spaces (see
https://github.com/leanprover-community/project-intentions/issues/15),
but I'm not sure how ongoing this is (Michael Rothgang ).
Thanks, Moritz Doll has already replied to me (in the Madrid channel), as have others whom I will reply to separately.

Generally though, upstreaming a big amount of LLM code to mathlib is not well liked and rarely (if ever) done for a variety of reasons.

Yes, I am already aware of that. But I think most of us are mathematicians first and software engineers second.
That is why it seems sensible to me to use an LLM as an aid. But of course the code first needs to be understood and properly documented. The central question, then, is this:
if one wants to modify this code so that it becomes acceptable, are there any guidelines? More generally, how can one distinguish LLM-generated code from human-written code?

Recently, I have been using an LLM to generalise some Emacs Lisp code (where I have the most experience). The result is often somewhat cumbersome, but perfectly readable.

Regards

The point is that we put a lot of value in the pedagogical significance of contributing to Mathlib. So we want that newcomers really try learning both lean and mathlib by going through the human experience of writing code, even if initially bad and at a slow pace. So, beyond the code being acceptable, we encourage contributions that lead to some learning. Also, reviewing a PR is a long a time-consuming process, and we don't want to spend this time trying to teach something to an LLM.

Let me also emphasize that mathlib has a very high quality bar for new contributions (both in terms of mathematical generality, abstract, and code quality). LLM-generated code, despite getting better, usually falls short of that bar. Put differently: one key outcome of humans in the loop during formalisation is understanding better how to formalise something well. (If I just wanted any formalisation I'd pour tokens into an LLM and spend my days hiking in the mountains instead.)

I understand that perfectly, but two points:

  1. Mathematically: is the greatest possible level of generality being sought? For example, should Sobolev spaces W^{s,p} be defined straight away for s∈ ℝ, rather than starting with W^{k,p} for k ∈ ℕ?
  2. More generally, what should one look out for in code, particularly as a beginner? Can LLM-generated code be cleaned up?
  3. I will ask Armstrong directly, but if I post a piece of the code here, perhaps someone could explain precisely what is wrong with such code.

A manual on «good programming in Lean» or «how to clean up LLM-generated code» would be very helpful.
For starters, do you even read the message you posted here? Do you realize how hard it is to read it due to the incorrect code formatting? (edit: the message above was edited afterwards)

Another formatting tip: do you know that you can write LaTeX by surrounding it in double dollar signs? (So, for example, $$W^{k,p}$$ would render as LaTeX?) Not strictly required, but I find it easier to re-read even my own messages that way.

I would, however, strongly recommend that whoever is responsible for configuring the system disable or clarify the email option mentioned in this message.

This is a good point. I agree the current way can be misleading. I have brought it up on #Zulip meta.
Regarding generality: indeed, we should aim for W^{s,p} for real s (and one of the first change we will make is this generalisation).
ok I will keep this this doble dollar trick in mind. However, if I use email and HTML, then Wp,sW^{p,s}Wp,s is converted to a png, which I am not sure, everybody would like.

Regarding generality: is done on Ω⊂Rn\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^nΩ⊂Rn? Do you know any functional space in mathlib4, (say even L2L^2L2 which is done on Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn or is everything done on Ω⊂Rn\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^nΩ⊂Rn

@Uwe Brauer if you want to write LLM-generated mathematics in order to grow a formal theory of differential equations more quickly or in less generality than mathlib (which is a perfectly reasonable thing to want), then you might want to consider a downstream library rather than mathlib itself. One LLM-friendly library aiming to cover mathematics much more broadly than mathlib is Tau Ceti https://taucetiproject.github.io/TauCeti/ . The mathlib model of formalisation is largely manual with more of a focus on doing things in "the right generality" and is quite happy to spend months thinking about what this generality is -- it is more like an academic research project studying ways to write mathematics in dependent type theory. It is not "let's get as much important stuff in as quickly as possible", that kind of "move fast and break stuff" attitude is far closer to Tau Ceti's take on formalisation. Here for example is what's going on with partial differential equations in Tau Ceti.

Uwe Brauer said:

Regarding generality: is done on Ω⊂Rn\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^nΩ⊂Rn? Do you know any functional space in mathlib4, (say even L2L^2L2 which is done on Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn or is everything done on Ω⊂Rn\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^nΩ⊂Rn

MeasureTheory.Lp is defined over any measurable space.

@Uwe Brauer Another point concerning your "starting with Wk,pW^{k,p}Wk,p for k∈Nk\in \mathbb{N}k∈N" is that actually generalising stuff is typically painful in the formalisation world. So, even if it seems easier to treat a special/simple case first, this often comes with a high price, that of refactoring everything afterwards. So often our attitude of seeking the greatest possible generality is a way of making our life easier, as counterintuitive this might sound.

I know that this is the argument which mathlib always gives, but it depends on what your goal is. For example our definition of manifold is carefully constructed so that it covers manifolds with boundary, manifolds with corners, infinite-dimensional manifolds, p-adic manifolds, infinite-dimensional p-adic manifolds and more. If your goal is to be Bourbaki++ (which I believe is one of mathlib's goals, at least implicitly; we maintainers play our cards close to our chest when it comes to stating goals of mathlib) then this is clearly the right thing to do. But if your goal is to, say, formalize the proof of the Poincare conjecture and then stop, then this definition of manifold makes your life slightly more difficult because it is too general for the task at hand. One has to find the right balance here, and it is perfectly reasonable that different people will have different opinions over the right generality. This is one of the reasons that we close so many LLM-generated PRs from mathlib -- the LLMs do not understand these basic mathlib principles yet and develop things in what looks like a reasonable generality but the maintainers and reviewers have different ideas.

Although this sounds persuasive at first sight, I would be rather cautious about the principle of «one ring to rule them all».

One could then reasonably ask why the spaces should be defined only for Ω⊂Rn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^nΩ⊂Rn, rather than for an arbitrary manifold, and then, in addition, for Ω\OmegaΩ subject to boundary conditions.

One could also consider weighted Sobolev spaces, either with a single weight function for all derivatives or with a different weight function for each derivative.

I am not sure that such a definition would remain particularly
tractable...

thanks! Good to know

Uwe Brauer said:

One could then reasonably ask why the spaces should be defined only for Ω⊂Rn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^nΩ⊂Rn, rather than for an arbitrary manifold [...]

How would you go about doing sobolev spaces over a manifold without first doing them over an open subset of Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn?

One could then reasonably ask why the spaces should be defined only for Ω⊂Rn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^nΩ⊂Rn, rather than for an arbitrary manifold, and then, in addition, for Ω\OmegaΩ subject to boundary conditions.

Indeed, I also dearly care about vector bundles of Sobolev class, and mathlib should include them. However, the way to define them is to define Sobolev space on a normed space (e.g. R^n) first, therefore we should have both. (This is a pattern very similar to the derivative of maps between normed spaces docs#fderiv and manifolds docs#mfderiv. Both are useful, and it is more convenient to use the former when you don't need the latter. So mathlib has both.)
And indeed, we should also do it over sets with nice boundary (for suitable values of "nice"). This is also planned.

Weighted Sobolev spaces: indeed, this should be considered carefully before committing to a design in mathlib. Deciding if the weighted and non-weighted case are sufficiently similar to be treated in a unified way, or sufficiently different to warrant separate development (with each setting informed by the other) will be part of the process of getting Sobolev spaces into mathlib.

The outcome of such a discussion depends on the setting. More often, there is a common generalisation (in which case we prefer to prove everything once in that setting, over duplicating all the proofs). Sometimes, the similarities are more superficial (e.g., finite vs infinite places in a number field) --- is such a case, having separate notions is appropriate.

Luigi Massacci said:

How would you go about doing sobolev spaces over a manifold without first doing them over an open subset of Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn?

You could define Wk,pW^{k,p}Wk,p on a Riemannian manifold directly. The downside is that you need a measure to do integration by parts.

My thoughts on the HsH^sHs scale on manifolds are to start with local HsH^sHs spaces (probably just as a predicate on distributions), this does not need a measure at all and in the case that the manifold is compact this is equivalent to global HsH^sHs. The case of non-compact manifolds is more involved any way.

Uwe Brauer said

One could think also about Besov spaces which have some advantage over Bessel spaces, if I recall correctly

I think Bessel potential is a special case of Triebel-Lizorkin (similar definition to Besov, just the sequence norm and the frequency norm are interchanged); Sobolev-Slobodeckij is a special case of Besov. All of these spaces would be great to have. I think having definitions for the more classical spaces is still good as their do appear way more frequently and the equivalence is not all trivial. Moreover, the norm on the abstract spaces is highly non-unique, whereas for the classical spaces you have a canonical norm.

Even though I agree with what Filippo said, I also think that finding the right generality is a process. We will not figure that out solely by discussing various abstract spaces. Someone has to actually get their hands dirty and write some Lean code and figure out what bits are hard, what works, what doesn't, etc.
There are also practical concerns similar to what Kevin said: if we would put all our effort into doing the utmost generality from the start, then it would take us forever to get to any practical result that your average PDE person would care about. When I started doing Lean there were normed spaces and Hilbert spaces, but not locally convex topological vector spaces, so I (together with Anatole Dedecker and Jireh Loreaux) put in quite some effort to get LCTVS in mathlib, but while that has been done, there is still a lot of results stated for normed spaces that hold in LCTVS and that need to be generalized. However, I don't think that mathlib would be better of if it had started with LCTVS.
